questions.question: Which five components make up the Transaction Manager?
options: Parser, optimizer, executor, buffer manager, storage engine
Scheduler, lock manager, write-ahead log, deadlock detector, recovery manager
Query router, cache, replication manager, index manager, vacuum
Scheduler, MVCC engine, checkpoint daemon, connection pool, planner
questions.explanation: The TM orchestrates scheduling, locking, write-ahead logging, deadlock detection, and recovery as one cooperating system, turning concurrent transactions into one consistent ACID state. Parser/optimizer/executor are the query-processing pipeline, a different subsystem.

questions.question: Mickey, Minnie, and Daffy run three concurrent transactions that touch entirely different tuples. Which TM component has nothing to do in this trace?
options: The scheduler, because no interleaving decisions are needed
The write-ahead log, because non-conflicting changes need no logging
The deadlock detector, because with no shared rows there are no waits, so the waits-for graph can never form a cycle
The lock manager, because non-overlapping rows need no locks
questions.explanation: Five components, four firing: the scheduler still routes transactions, the lock manager still grants (non-blocking) locks, and the WAL still logs every change before commit. Only the deadlock detector idles, since deadlock requires transactions waiting on each other, which needs shared rows.

questions.question: According to the scaling analysis, why can a Transaction Manager run about a million transactions per second on commodity hardware?
options: Most transactions touch independent rows (only ~10-20 of ~1,000 conflict), lock checks are O(1) hash lookups, and the WAL turns scattered updates into one sequential stream
Modern CPUs execute each transaction on its own dedicated core
The TM batches all transactions into one big transaction per second
Locks are skipped entirely for read-only transactions, which dominate the workload
questions.explanation: The throughput comes from three design choices: most transactions never wait because they never conflict, each lock check is a constant-time hash lookup, and logging is sequential. Separation of concerns keeps each component behind a tiny interface. Batching and per-core dedication are not the mechanisms the course describes.

questions.question: In the three-transaction trace, T3 aborts while T1 and T2 commit. Why don't T1 and T2 have to roll back too?
options: Because T1 and T2 committed before T3 started, so the schedule was serial
Because the recovery manager re-ran T1 and T2 after undoing T3
Because T3 only performed reads, which never need undoing
Under Strict 2PL, T3 held its exclusive locks on B and C until it ended, so no other transaction ever read its uncommitted data; the abort is contained and never cascades
questions.explanation: This is the 'strict' in Strict 2PL earning its name: no one builds on T3's dirty values because T3 never released its locks before aborting. The schedule was interleaved, not serial, and T3 wrote both B and C; containment comes from lock discipline, not from timing luck or read-only status.

questions.question: Start state A=19, B=32, C=27. All-commit ends at A=27.36, B=38.4, C=32.4. In Scenario 2, T1 and T2 (which share A) commit but T3 (which wrote B and C) aborts. What is the final state, and how is it reached?
options: A=19, B=32, C=27: an abort anywhere rolls the database back to the start state
A=27.36, B=32, C=27: the recovery manager reads T3's WAL entries backward and restores the old values of C and B, leaving T1 and T2's committed work on A untouched
A=27.36, B=38.4, C=32.4: aborts only matter if the server also crashes
A=19, B=38.4, C=32.4: T3's writes survive but the shared counter A reverts
questions.explanation: Undo is per-transaction: walking T3's WAL entries backward reverts C from 32.4 to 27 and B from 38.4 to 32, while A keeps both committed updates (27.36). Rolling back the whole database would violate durability for T1 and T2; atomicity only erases the transaction that failed.

questions.question: What is the core design flaw in the Ticketdisaster.com checkout flow?
options: The virtual queue admits users in random order instead of first-come-first-served
The database lacks a write-ahead log, so crashes lose purchases
It locks an entire zone (1,000+ seats) the moment a user picks it and holds the lock through browsing and payment, so one slow user freezes thousands of seats for minutes
Payment processing runs inside the OS kernel, starving the lock manager
questions.explanation: The lock is both too big (a whole zone) and held too long (through a human typing card details, 5-10 minutes). The transaction machinery itself is correct; the application's use of it is what falls over under load, which is the page's whole point.

questions.question: Ticketsfaster.com switches from zone-level locks (1,000 seats) to seat-level locks (1-8 seats). Why does this raise concurrent users from ~100 to ~10,000?
options: Smaller locks are faster for the lock manager to grant, cutting per-lock latency
Seat-level locks are shared rather than exclusive, so buyers no longer wait
Higher-resolution locking means lower contention: locking one seat blocks nobody else, so thousands of fans browse and buy different seats at once
Fewer locked rows means the WAL writes fewer entries per purchase
questions.explanation: The win is contention, not lock overhead: a zone lock blocks 999 other fans behind one user, while a seat lock blocks essentially no one. The locks are still exclusive for the purchase; there are just vastly fewer buyers who need the same one.

questions.question: What is Strategy 2's key move for cutting lock duration from 5-10 minutes to about 30 seconds?
options: Move the slow human steps (browsing, typing card number and billing address) outside the critical section: pre-fill everything in the queue with no lock held, then take the lock only for the final write
Replace the human payment step with a stored credit-card vault that charges automatically
Give each user a hard 30-second timer, after which their lock is revoked
Process payments on a faster network so card authorization completes sooner
questions.explanation: The slowest part of checkout is a human typing, and none of it needs a lock. Collecting it up front in the queue shrinks the locked window to just the final confirm-and-write. A revocation timer is the old broken design (the timeout that kicked users back to the queue), not the fix.

questions.question: Even with seat-level, short-duration locks, load can still overwhelm real-time locking. What is Strategy 3, and what problem of the old flow does it dissolve?
options: Add read replicas so seat-availability reads never touch the primary
Shard the seat map across servers so no one lock manager is a bottleneck
Cache seat availability aggressively and let occasional double-sells be refunded later

Fall back to an async timestamp system: fans submit requests instantly, a background job processes them in timestamp order and emails confirmations, replacing blocking waits, and eliminating the uncertain reserved-but-not-purchased state that pending payments create
questions.explanation: When blocking is unavoidable, make the wait predictable and transparent: a stamped submission queue turns a 3-hour lock-holding wait into a 60-second submit and scales to ~50,000 concurrent users. Caching with double-sells sacrifices the correctness guarantee the whole module is built to keep.

questions.question: In the nested correctness rings (Serializable ⊃ Conflict-Serializable ⊃ 2PL ⊃ Strict 2PL), where does the course say the next 100x of throughput lives?
options: In tuning Strict 2PL itself to grant locks faster
In the rings outside Strict 2PL: perfectly safe, serializable schedules that today's S2PL databases refuse to run
In relaxing the correctness target so non-serializable schedules become acceptable
In faster hardware, since protocols are already optimal
questions.explanation: Every ring outside S2PL contains valid schedules a smarter scheduler could admit; that untapped gap is the opportunity. Crucially, the correctness target never moves, serializable stays the bar; only the scheduler changes. Tuning 2PL itself is explicitly the dead-end path.

questions.question: A song lands 10 million plays in an hour, pure write throughput on an append-heavy stream. Which protocol matches this workload signature?
options: Micro-locking: lock the single play-count field instead of the whole row
Timestamp ordering: run every play in timestamp order and abort conflicts
LSM trees: append every write to an immutable file with no locks at all, with reads that settle a moment later (ClickHouse, BigQuery, Snowflake)
Strict 2PL with a larger lock table
questions.explanation: Read the signature, and the protocol falls out: pure write throughput wants lock-free appends, which is LSM trees. Micro-locking fits fine-grained contention on one hot counter (Postgres, SQL Server, Oracle), and timestamp ordering fits global ordering across agents (Spanner).

questions.question: Why can a scheduler that admits schedules which are serializable but NOT conflict-serializable still be correct?
options: Because what defines correct is serializability, equal to some serial order; conflict-serializability is only the mechanical test 2PL happens to pass, so schedules outside CS but inside Serializable are still safe headroom
Because conflict-serializability was proven equivalent to serializability, so the two rings are the same
Because such schedules only involve read-only transactions, which cannot conflict
It cannot; anything outside conflict-serializable is unsafe by definition
questions.explanation: CS is a sufficient, checkable stand-in for serializability, not the definition of it: the rings nest strictly, and the Serializable-minus-CS gap is real, safe schedules. Believing CS is correctness is exactly the misconception this page dismantles; the target stays serializability while the scheduler gets smarter.
